video_title: Another bipartisan housing miracle, this time in Idaho
gist: Idaho Republican state senator Ben Taves and Boise Democrat Megan Eggert walk through the six deregulatory housing bills their state passed in 2026 — by-right ADUs, 500-square-foot minimum lot sizes for starter-home subdivisions, manufactured homes in single-family zones, single-stair apartments, a six-day permitting shot clock and lot splits — plus the duplex and YIGBY bills that died 7-7 in House Business. The recurring structural obstacle is not zoning but HB389, Idaho's 2021 property tax cap, which makes growth fiscally punishing for cities and may let them invoke infrastructure opt-outs against the very reforms just passed.

insights.claim: Idaho passed six housing deregulation bills in the 2026 session out of roughly eight introduced, covering ADUs by right, starter-home subdivisions, manufactured homes in single-family zones, single-stair apartment buildings, a permitting shot clock, and lot splits.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: A red state stacking six supply-side reforms at once is the template other Mountain West legislatures copy; watch Idaho starts and lot absorption as the first read on whether preemption actually moves volume.

insights.claim: SB1354 makes accessory dwelling units buildable by right on residential property in Idaho cities and strips cities of the power to block them.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator, Idaho District 4)
insights.so_what: By-right ADU statutes are the highest-velocity unit-count reform available; suppliers of small-format modular units, kit homes and detached-ADU packages get a new statewide addressable market.
insights.quote: That specific bill gives homeowners or property owners the ability to build an ADU on their property by right uh and stops the cities from stopping from stopping those builds.

insights.claim: SB1352 lets starter-home subdivisions be platted on parcels of four acres or more and bars cities from imposing minimum lot sizes above 500 square feet, allowing densities up to 12 homes per acre.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Lot size is the binding cost constraint the senator names explicitly, so land developers with 4+ acre Idaho holdings just saw a step-change in permissible yield per acre.

insights.claim: Land cost is one of the largest single components of a single-family home in Idaho, which is why minimum-lot-size caps rather than subsidies were the lever chosen to make small homes pencil.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Where dirt dominates cost structure, density reform expands builder gross margin faster than any input-price move; screen builders by lot-cost share to find who benefits most.
insights.quote: obviously the dirt is like one of the biggest costs of a of a single family residence

insights.claim: Idaho now allows modern manufactured homes by right in areas zoned for single-family housing, on the argument that today's product is visually indistinguishable from stick-built.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Zoning parity is the classic unlock for manufactured-housing penetration; watch factory-built shipment share in Idaho as a leading indicator for the same statute spreading.

insights.claim: HB706 legalized single-stair apartment buildings in Idaho conditional on sprinklers and other safety systems, passing by a single vote against firefighter opposition.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Single-stair reform materially improves small-lot multifamily floorplate efficiency; a one-vote margin means the coalition is fragile and reversal risk is real in a turnover year.
insights.quote: It passed by one vote.

insights.claim: Idaho's permitting shot clock gives cities six days to issue a permit, after which the applicant may hire a third-party inspector and the city must refund the permit fee — and it passed unanimously.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: A unanimous vote plus a self-executing private remedy makes this the most durable of the six reforms and the one most likely to be copied verbatim elsewhere; third-party inspection firms gain a mandated fallback role.

insights.claim: Roughly 25% of the cost of a new Idaho home is now attributable to the municipal approval process itself, according to legislative estimates cited in the session.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: If a quarter of delivered cost is process, procedural reform is a bigger margin lever than lumber or labor — size builder upside off entitlement friction, not commodity inputs.
insights.quote: around 25% they're estimating around 25% of homes now are the cost is in, you know, the whole process with the cities

insights.claim: Idaho's lot-split bill exists mainly as a financing mechanism, letting an ADU sit on its own legal parcel so banks can underwrite it as a separate loan.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Zoning permission without financeability produces no units; the parcelization workaround is the tell that ADU volume depends on lender product, creating an opening for specialty ADU-lending originators.
insights.quote: it's a financing mechanism to allow a lot split to uh make it easier to finance like an ADU on your property

themes.theme: Dillon's rule as the preemption lever

insights.claim: Idaho operates under Dillon's rule, meaning municipal powers are granted by the state rather than constitutionally held, which the bill sponsor treats as the legal justification for statewide preemption of local land use rules.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Dillon's-rule states are the low-friction path for statewide zoning preemption; use that legal status as the screen for which states can plausibly replicate Idaho's package.
insights.quote: Idaho operates based on something called Dylan's rule. Uh, essentially any local municipality, whatever power they have is actually granted to them by the state.

insights.claim: The interim committee's statewide travel neutralized the local-control objection by demonstrating that housing scarcity showed up identically in Boise, Coeur d'Alene and rural Idaho rather than being a big-city problem.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative, Boise)
insights.so_what: The reproducible political mechanism here is evidence-gathering that reframes a local issue as statewide — the precondition for preemption bills to survive committee.
insights.quote: Local control makes a lot of sense when something is simply a local problem. This this is not this was impacting the entire state

insights.claim: Idaho's 2025 interim land use and housing study committee was directly modeled on Montana's, showing that state-level housing reform is now propagating between red states by imitation.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Policy diffusion across neighboring red states is faster than expected; front-run the next adopters by watching which legislatures convene interim housing committees.

insights.claim: Deliberately assembling realtors, home builders, a developer, the apartment association and city administrators alongside legislators from both parties produced a package that passed, because industry was inside the drafting room rather than lobbying against it from outside.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Coalition composition predicts bill survival better than partisan control; the absence of industry from a state's housing committee is a signal its reforms will stall.

insights.claim: The reform package's applicability threshold was raised from cities of 5,000 residents to cities of 10,000, a concession the sponsor accepted because it let legislators whose districts contain no city that large vote yes without local blowback.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Population thresholds are the cheapest currency in housing preemption fights — they cost little real coverage and buy rural votes; expect the same trade in every copycat state.

insights.claim: Counties were excluded from the scope of Idaho's housing bills purely as a vote-buying concession, which the sponsor concedes removed one major organization from the opposition.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: The county carve-out leaves unincorporated exurban land largely untouched, so the near-term development unlock is inside city limits and 'areas of impact', not raw county acreage.
insights.quote: It took one major organization off off the fight.

insights.claim: On ADUs, existing HOAs cannot revoke the right to build without unanimous member consent, but newly formed HOAs may still prohibit ADUs outright — and roughly 90% of new homes in Idaho are being built inside HOAs.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: The new-HOA carve-out is a structural leak: if 90% of new product is HOA-governed, developers can simply covenant ADUs away, capping the statute's effect on future subdivisions.
insights.quote: somebody told me that around 90% of the homes that are being built are in HOAs

insights.claim: The sponsor explicitly runs an incrementalist strategy — narrow a bill only as far as needed to pass, then expand its scope in later sessions — and has already named areas of impact and counties as the next expansion targets.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Treat the 2026 package as a floor, not a ceiling; the stated roadmap means geographic scope expansion is the base case for the 2027 session.
insights.quote: the na the natural next step when you're doing incremental uh legislation is you narrow it to what uh will get it done and then you just expand it

insights.claim: Accepting every amendment demanded by opponents on the duplex bill still failed to move them to neutral, leading the sponsor to conclude that some opposition is not negotiable in good faith.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Where opposition is positional rather than substantive, concession strategies burn scope for nothing — a reason to expect future Idaho bills to be less amended, not more.
insights.quote: I took every amendment they asked for on the twin home duplex bill and I expected them to go neutral or to support it and they still opposed it

insights.claim: Idaho's duplex bill, which would have barred HOAs, cities and counties from banning duplexes anywhere single-family homes are allowed, died on a 7-7 tie in the House Business Committee despite passing the Senate strongly.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Missing-middle legalization is the harder ask even in a legislature that just legalized ADUs and 500-square-foot lots; a one-vote committee swing in an election year flips it.

insights.claim: Idaho's YIGBY bill would have allowed multifamily and mixed-use development by right on land owned or leased by religious organizations while capping height restrictions, setbacks and parking minimums, and it also died 7-7 in House Business.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Church-land supply is an unusually large latent land bank in Idaho, and the bill also targets parking minimums and height caps — a broader multifamily unlock than its framing implies.

insights.claim: The YIGBY bill failed mainly because legislators wrongly believed it would authorize homeless shelters, meaning its 2027 prospects hinge on committee education rather than substantive redrafting.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Misinformation-driven failures reverse faster than interest-driven ones; a bill that died on misunderstanding is a higher-probability 2027 pass than one that died on lobbying.

insights.claim: The only substantive argument raised against duplex legalization was that duplexes depress neighboring property values, a claim the Democratic committee member dismisses as absurd given duplexes are physically equivalent to houses and reduce per-unit infrastructure cost.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Property-value anxiety, not fire safety or infrastructure, is the real blocker on missing middle — a signal that homeowner wealth psychology is the binding political constraint nationally.

themes.theme: HB389 property tax cap as the hidden growth brake

insights.claim: Idaho's 2021 House Bill 389 caps growth in city property tax revenue, so a city approving a new subdivision absorbs infrastructure costs immediately while the offsetting tax revenue arrives later and in capped form — making rapid growth fiscally punishing for municipalities.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: This is the structural reason Idaho cities resist growth; municipal credit and utility-district finance in fast-growing Idaho cities carry a squeeze that zoning reform does not fix.

insights.claim: Every bill in the package lets a city opt out by showing it cannot support the required infrastructure, which combined with the HB389 revenue cap arguably gives cities a near-automatic mathematical escape hatch from the reforms.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: The single biggest execution risk to the whole package is an interaction between two unrelated statutes; watch how many cities invoke the infrastructure exemption after February 1.

insights.claim: The Republican sponsor of the housing package openly wants HB389's property tax cap reversed or loosened for fast-growing areas, endorsing the 'growth should pay for itself' principle against his own party's anti-tax flank.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: A visible intra-Republican split between pro-supply and anti-tax factions is the fault line to track for whether Idaho's reforms actually produce units.
insights.quote: I think it doesn't make sense at all in the in the case where an area is growing quickly

insights.claim: Two bills to loosen Idaho's property tax cap died this session — including HB842, which would have roughly doubled the ceiling — with the Idaho Freedom Foundation mobilizing to kill them, and the fix is believed to have died on the House side.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host) and Megan Eggert
insights.so_what: An organized anti-tax group can veto the fiscal precondition for housing supply even when the housing bills themselves pass; the binding constraint is revenue, not zoning.

insights.claim: The property tax cap is already straining Idaho ambulance and fire districts, and the legislature has been passing band-aid fixes that the sponsor says cannot substitute for major reform.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves and Megan Eggert
insights.so_what: Special-district fiscal stress in a high-growth state is an early warning for service-level deterioration and eventual forced tax reform — relevant to Idaho muni exposure.
insights.quote: there was band-aids being set sent over to us to try to fix all of the issues and it's like a it's a bigger issue than a band-aid's going to fix

insights.claim: Both legislators expect the 2026 election to be the mechanism that changes the House's appetite on the property tax cap, framing the fiscal fix as a post-election rather than intra-session event.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: The catalyst calendar for Idaho's fiscal fix is November 2026, not the February session — sequence any thesis on Idaho municipal capacity accordingly.

themes.theme: Regulation-only reform and the missing subsidy leg

insights.claim: None of the interim committee's subsidy or financial-incentive recommendations became law; only the zero-cost regulatory reforms advanced, partly because Idaho made drastic mid-fiscal-year statewide budget cuts.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Fiscal stress, not just ideology, is what selects for deregulation over subsidy — the same filter is likely operating in other states facing revenue shortfalls.

insights.claim: The Democratic committee member argues regulatory reform alone will not solve Idaho housing and frames it as a multi-year adaptive problem with no single legislative fix.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Expect a multi-session drip of Idaho housing legislation rather than a one-time catalyst; position for cumulative rather than step-function supply response.
insights.quote: It's going to take everything. It's going to take everything for multiple years, trying different things, adapting it as we learn more.

insights.claim: The likely form of any future Idaho housing money is tax breaks or incentives for landowners who deed-restrict affordability, not direct government subsidy or giveaways.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert and Ben Taves
insights.so_what: If Idaho ever funds affordability it will be through the tax code and deed restrictions — a structure that favors developers able to hold restricted inventory, not LIHTC-style syndication.

insights.claim: Kit-built homes now being delivered by semi truck and assembled in 21 days are selling in Idaho for around $300,000, which the sponsor cites as evidence the market is already responding without state money.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: A $300k delivered price against a $550k regional average is the cost gap that makes factory-built the marginal supplier once zoning permits it; watch modular/kit builders entering Idaho.
insights.quote: They they literally drive a semi with everything to build a house. They can build it in 21 days.

insights.claim: Idaho nonprofits are running revolving down-payment assistance funds that are replenished when the assisted buyer later sells, which the Republican sponsor prefers over public subsidy.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Shared-appreciation style revolving funds are the politically viable affordability vehicle in anti-subsidy states; a replicable structure for philanthropic and CDFI capital.

insights.claim: Cities repeatedly told the sponsor that if real demand for small starter homes existed the market would already be meeting it, an argument he says is directly falsified by what is now being built once rules changed.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: The 'no demand' defense is the standard municipal rationale for restrictive zoning; its rapid falsification in Idaho is the empirical case study reformers elsewhere will cite.
insights.quote: I was told over and over again I'm um that from the cities and from different people if there was really demand, you know, it would be taken care of. Well, no, it's that's not the case.

insights.claim: Idaho cities have until February 1 to bring local codes into compliance with the new housing laws, and the sponsor expects the real risk is not open defiance but cities finding fresh loopholes to keep blocking projects.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: February 1, 2027 compliance filings are the concrete checkpoint for whether these statutes translate into permits; loophole behavior would push the real supply response out by years.
insights.quote: I'm actually not as concerned that they'll ignore it completely as they'll find other loopholes that they can use to block it.

insights.claim: Idaho's primary enforcement mechanism against non-complying cities is private developer litigation, with state tax transfers to cities held in reserve as a secondary lever the sponsor hopes not to use.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Litigation-dependent enforcement means the reforms bind only where a developer has capital and appetite to sue — favoring larger builders over small local operators.

insights.claim: Some Idaho cities are privately relieved by state preemption because it lets them do what local vocal-minority opposition prevented them from doing themselves.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: State preemption functions as political cover for cooperative municipalities, which means compliance may be broader than the public local-control fight suggests.

insights.claim: Housing hearings systematically over-represent a vocal minority because the working families who would benefit cannot attend city council meetings and often do not know they are in the beneficiary constituency at all.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves and David Roberts
insights.so_what: The structural asymmetry between concentrated opposition and diffuse, unaware beneficiaries explains why housing reform must be done at the state level rather than locally.

insights.claim: Statewide polling shows housing reform polls very highly in Idaho with roughly ten supporters for every hearing-room opponent, which the sponsor expects to eventually translate into electoral pressure on mayors and city councils.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: If housing becomes a ballot-box issue rather than a hearing-room one, local resistance decays; municipal election results are the leading indicator for compliance behavior.

themes.theme: Ownership vs rental: the horizontal density thesis

insights.claim: The Republican sponsor distinguishes 'horizontal density' — more owner-occupied homes built closer together — from 'vertical density' meaning rental apartments, and explicitly prefers the former because ownership builds equity and roots residents in communities.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: This framing predicts which reforms a red-state legislature will pass: for-sale small-lot and ADU product advances while multifamily rental bills stall, skewing the supply response toward single-family-for-sale.
insights.quote: that's why I'm such a proponent of what I call horizontal density. like I'm like if we have to build houses closer together fine but um but people need a way to put down roots

insights.claim: The average American now buys a first home after age 40, versus the sponsor's own purchase at 24, a generational shift he treats as the core political argument for the whole package.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: A 16-year delay in first purchase compresses the lifetime equity accumulation that underpins US household wealth — a structural headwind for consumer balance sheets and a political tailwind for supply reform.
insights.quote: the average age when somebody buys their first house now is over 40 years old

insights.claim: Because most American household wealth sits in the primary residence, homeowners rationally fight any new supply they fear could reduce their property value — and the sponsor observed legislators in both chambers appearing to vote based on their own homes rather than their constituents'.
insights.speaker: David Roberts and Ben Taves
insights.so_what: Voting patterns cut across party lines and track personal housing exposure, so partisan control is a poor predictor of housing-reform outcomes in any state.

insights.claim: The Boise Democrat argues that adding for-sale starter homes helps renters through pure supply-and-demand rather than requiring renter-specific policy, aligning her with the free-market Republicans on mechanism if not emphasis.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Bipartisan convergence on supply as the mechanism is what makes these coalitions stable; it also means rent-control-style interventions are off the table in Idaho.
insights.quote: I am kind of a purist when it comes to supply and demand here.

insights.claim: Boise specifically must build up rather than out because the alternative consumes public land and raises infrastructure and commuting costs, and its pre-war neighborhoods already demonstrate that higher density works there.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: Idaho's capital is the one market where multifamily infill demand is structurally supported, making Boise the divergent submarket from the statewide for-sale tilt.

insights.claim: Restrictive minimum lot sizes such as 8,500 square feet are counterproductive, pushing households out to areas with no infrastructure and worsening the sprawl and service costs the rules were meant to prevent.
insights.speaker: Megan Eggert (Democratic state representative)
insights.so_what: The feedback loop from large-lot zoning to exurban infrastructure cost is the fiscal argument that converts growth-skeptic officials — the most transferable talking point in the episode.

insights.claim: The sponsor's own 20-unit small-home project, planned at 700–1,200 square feet and priced around $300,000 against a regional average of $550,000, was killed when the city imposed new green space requirements at PUD renewal — the direct origin of the legislation.
insights.speaker: Ben Taves (Republican state senator)
insights.so_what: Retroactive rule changes at entitlement renewal are an underappreciated project-killing risk; it is also the mechanism by which developer-legislators become housing reformers.
insights.quote: the city came back to us and we went to renew the PUD and they said, "Uh, sorry, you can't do that. Um, there's new green space requirements and your plans don't uh match those requirements."
